content.text:
**Choice: candidate 1.** It is only slightly ahead of candidate 2, so this is a close call. I worked it out by hand with rough approximations, not a simulation.

**What every plan loses the same way.** Every plan's first delivery arrives on day 3 for product 0 and day 2 for product 1. The starting stock (58 and 26) can't cover the first days' demand (about 121 and 37 units), so every plan has about the same early shortfall. This doesn't separate them.

**Biweekly plans (0, 1, 2, 5, 7): how the costs net out.** Leftover stock carries over to the next cycle, so the safety stock builds up over time. For product 0, profit ≈ 19·demand − 12·ordered − 25·units short − storage. For product 1, it is 11·demand − 5·ordered − 16·units short − storage. I treated the cumulative "demand minus deliveries" as a random walk: about σ ≈ 20 per 2-day cycle for product 0 and about 7.5 for product 1. The mean multiplier of 1.046 adds a drift on top. Under that model, the expected maximum of the walk gives the expected shortfall.

- **Candidate 1** orders exactly the forecast (1147 and 458 units). The 1.046 bias leaves it short about 78 units of product 0 and about 30 of product 1. Its average leftover stock is small, so storage costs little.
- **Candidate 2** orders about 1.10× the forecast. Shortfalls drop to about 23 and 8 units. For product 0, the extra purchase (115 × 12 ≈ 1380) roughly equals the penalty and lost revenue it avoids (55 × 25 ≈ 1375). But leftover stock builds to about 85 and 34 units by the end. That costs about 250 more in product 0 storage and about 290 more in product 1 storage (0.9 per unit per day), and whatever is left at the end is wasted.
- Overall, candidate 1 comes out about 400 ahead of candidate 2.
- **Candidates 5, 7 and 0** (1.15–1.25×) cut the shortfall only a little more. They pay 12 per extra unit, carry much more stock, and spill units at the 224-unit warehouse limit. That makes them clearly worse.

**Daily plans (4, 6).** They pay the fixed 53 fee on 28 days instead of 14, which is about 742 more. Holding less stock between deliveries saves only about 390. So candidate 4 (exactly the forecast) is about 350 below candidate 1, and candidate 6 (about 1.14×) is worse still.

**Every-three-days plan (3).** Ordering less often saves about 265 in fees. But each delivery covers three days, so average stock is higher and storage costs about 370 more. Its large deliveries also go over the 224-unit limit (for example, around days 18–19). It ends up no better than candidate 2.

**How robust this is.** The shortfall cost goes up steeply as the order factor drops, so the best factor is probably somewhere between 1.0 and 1.1. Candidates 1 and 2 are about equally far from it. The storage costs and the end-of-horizon waste are what tip the balance to candidate 1.

I recommend **Candidate 2**. These are estimates I worked out by hand from the forecasts; nothing was simulated.

**What all plans share:** the opening stock can't be helped. Product 0 has 58 units against forecast demand of 121 for days 0–2. Product 1 has 26 against 37 for days 0–1. Every candidate loses about the same here.

**The key point:** goods keep longer than the gap between deliveries (8–9 days of shelf life against a 2–3 day cycle). So leftovers roll into the next cycle, and any safety margin built into each order adds up over the month. What matters is total quantity ordered compared with total expected demand. Expected demand is the forecast × 1.046, which is about 1,200 units of product 0 for days 3–29 and about 479 of product 1 for days 2–29.

- **Candidates 0 and 7** order 1,435 and 1,376 units of product 0. That's 175–235 units over expected demand. The extra stock goes unsold at the end or is lost when the 224-unit warehouse overflows (around days 19–20), at 12 per unit plus storage.
- **Candidate 5** front-loads a buffer (about 1.15× forecast, then cuts back at the end). That leaves around 100 extra units of product 0 by day 26 and about 90 at the end. It also pays more storage on product 1, which costs 0.9 per unit per day. On day 19 the 145-unit delivery arrives with that buffer on hand, so stock would reach about 245, over the 224 limit.
- **Candidate 1** orders exactly the forecast: 1,148 units of product 0 against about 1,200 expected. It runs short by about 50 units and is short again every time demand comes in above forecast. Each missed unit costs 13 (7 lost margin plus a 6 penalty).
- **Candidates 4 and 6** order every day, which costs 14 more order days × 53 = 742 in fixed fees. Candidate 4 also orders only the forecast amount, so it runs short too.
- **Candidate 3** orders every 3 days. That saves 5 × 53 = 265 in order fees, but the larger deliveries add about 380 in storage costs. On day 18 a 184-unit delivery of product 0 arrives while the warehouse already holds leftovers of both products. That's roughly 268 units against 224, so about 40 units would be lost.

**Candidate 2** orders about 1.1× forecast every 2 days. Its expected surplus at the end is about 60 units of product 0 and 25 of product 1. That roughly matches the best buffer when a missed sale costs 13 and an unsold unit costs about 12: around 0.7 standard deviations of total demand over the month, or 50 units. Its peak stock (about 207 on day 19) stays under the limit. It also holds up best when demand differs from the forecast: it rarely runs out and doesn't pile up much surplus.

**Choice: candidate 1.** It has the highest expected profit. Candidates 1 and 2 are the only close pair; everything was worked out by hand on forecast averages.

**1. How often to order.** Each ordering day costs 53.
- **Candidates 4 and 6 (daily):** 28 ordering days cost about 1484, against 742 for ordering every 2 days. Daily ordering saves roughly 400 in holding, so these two lose about 340 net.
- **Candidate 3 (every 3 days):** it saves 265 in order fees but adds about 400 in holding. It also overfills the 224-unit store around days 17–18 (about 184 of product 0 plus leftovers, plus product 1 stock), and the excess is lost.
- **The rest (0, 1, 2, 5, 7) order every 2 days.** Product 0 arrives on odd days and product 1 on even days, so they never compete for space on arrival.

**2. How much to order in total.** Shelf life is 8–9 days and sales take the oldest stock first, so a surplus rolls forward and almost never expires. It ends up as worthless stock at the end, and holding is paid on it every night. Shortfalls are lost for good.

| Product | Expected demand on ordered days (avg multiplier 1.046) | Cand. 1 | Cand. 2 | Cand. 5 | Cand. 7 | Cand. 0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | ≈ 1200 | 1147 | 1262 | 1290 | 1376 | 1435 |
| 1 | ≈ 479 | 458 | 505 | 512 | 458 | 576 |

- **Product 0:** an extra unit costs 12 plus holding, about 3 in total. If it gets sold it earns 25 (19 in sales plus the 6 penalty avoided). It pays off only if the chance it sells is above about 0.6. That puts the best total slightly below expected demand, around 1190.
  - Candidate 1 expects to miss about 70 sales and end with about 18 units left over.
  - Candidate 2 expects to miss about 18 sales but ends with about 80 left over and carries about 30 more units each night.
  - Overall, candidate 1 comes out about 300 ahead.
  - Candidates 7 and 0 overbuy by 180–235 units, losing about 12 each, and also risk overfilling the store around day 19.
- **Product 1:** a unit costs 5, a sale earns 16 (11 plus the 5 penalty avoided), and holding is a steep 0.9 per night. The best total is well below demand, roughly 445–475. Candidate 1 (458) is closest. Candidates 2 and 5 carry 15–20 extra units every night, which costs about 365 for a gain of about 150.

**3. Risk from random demand.** Candidate 1's shortfall per 2-day period is small: about 4 units on average, against swings of about 19. Losses grow evenly. The plans that overbuy are the ones exposed to sharp losses, mainly from overfilling the store (candidates 0, 7, 3).

**Ranking:** 1 > 2 ≈ 5 > 4 > 7 > 6, 3, 0.

I pick **candidate 1**, with about 0.4 confidence that it comes out best on actual demand. Candidate 2 is close behind. I did all the arithmetic by hand, so the estimates are rough.

**Losses every plan shares.** Stock of good 0 is 58 against about 127 units of demand on days 0–2. Stock of good 1 is 26 against about 39 on days 0–1. No plan can deliver earlier, so all of them start the cycle with an empty shelf and lose about 70 + 13 units of demand.

**How often to order.**
- **Every day (4 and 6):** 28 order days cost about 1484 in fees instead of 742. Smaller deliveries save only about 360 in storage. These plans are about 380 worse than the every-other-day plan with the same safety margin.
- **Every three days (3):** it saves 265 in fees but adds about 360 in storage. Around day 18 (184 units of good 0 plus leftovers) and day 27 it can also overflow the 224-unit warehouse. It is worse than candidate 2, which has the same 1.1× margin.

**The every-other-day plans (0, 1, 2, 5, 7).** These plans order fixed amounts and never react to what actually sold. Any order above the true average demand (about 1.046× the forecast) piles up as surplus. That surplus costs storage every day and is worth nothing at the end. Margins over the forecast:

| Plan | Good 0 | Good 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1.25× | 1.25× |
| 1 | 1.0× | 1.0× |
| 2 | 1.1× | 1.1× |
| 5 | about 1.15×, trimmed at the end | about 1.15×, trimmed at the end |
| 7 | 1.2× | 1.0× |

I estimated lost sales with a random-walk model of the stock (Spitzer's formula). The estimates come from these figures:
- Good 0: average shortfall of 4 units per two-day period, spread of about 19 units.
- Good 1: average shortfall of 1.5 units per period, spread of about 7.4 units.

| Plan | Good 0 lost | Good 0 left at end | Good 1 lost | Good 1 left at end | Profit after fees, before shared losses (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~81 | ~28 | ~31 | ~10 | **~8,800** |
| 2 | ~23 | ~85 | ~9 | ~35 | ~8,500 |
| 5 | ~12 | ~100 | ~5 | ~38 | ~8,100 |
| 7 | ~6 | ~180 | ~31 | ~10 | ~7,300 |
| 0 | ~3 | ~240, some overflow | ~1 | ~95 | ~5,300 |

Each extra unit ordered only prevents a lost sale about half the time. That saves about 12.5 for good 0 (13 for good 1). Against that, it costs 12 to buy (5 for good 1). If unsold, it also costs storage every day: 0.3 for good 0, 0.9 for good 1. So the extra margin doesn't pay off, and it pays off least for good 1 because its storage is so expensive.

**How sure.** Candidate 1 leads candidate 2 by only about 300. That gap is close to the error in these estimates. If actual demand runs above forecast, candidate 2 (or 5) wins; if it runs below, candidate 1 wins.
